question: A data service doubles its worker nodes but a global lock serializes every transaction. What is the most defensible performance prediction?
options: The global lock can still serialize work, so adding workers may leave throughput nearly unchanged
Twice the workers can bypass the shared lock by duplicating lock state across the cluster
The extra CPUs remove the sequential fraction once data are stored on different physical disks
Throughput should grow with worker count because the global lock cost is diluted when additional CPUs are available
explanation: A serial critical section limits speed-up and may dominate throughput. Horizontal scaling only helps when meaningful work can be partitioned and coordination costs remain manageable.
source: L9 Scalable Data Management slides 2-4 (scale-out, throughput and cloud elasticity).

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sharding from replication?
options: Sharding creates redundant copies for reads, while replication distributes distinct logical keys across nodes
Replication adds distinct records to the logical dataset, while sharding mainly increases read availability
Sharding divides distinct records across nodes; replication stores additional copies of existing records
Sharding and replication differ only in placement strategy; each necessarily duplicates the full table
explanation: Sharding partitions responsibility for records, while replication creates redundant copies for availability, locality or reads. They can be combined but have different capacity and consistency effects.
source: L9 slides 3-6 (shared-nothing/cloud distribution and storage); Özsu & Valduriez, Principles of Distributed Database Systems, ch. 10, pp. 449-456.

question: Two replicas are disconnected. DB1 accepts write x = 10; DB2 has x = 0. To preserve linearizable reads during the partition, what must DB2 avoid?
options: Failing a read rather than returning data when replicas cannot coordinate safely
Rejecting a read whose consistency requirements cannot be established with the currently reachable nodes
Blocking the request while obtaining evidence of the most recent completed write or safe serving state
Replying with stale x = 0 as the current value after DB1 has already completed the write x = 10
explanation: Serving x=0 after a completed x=10 write would violate the single-copy latest-value view if the write is ordered before the read. A CP-style choice can block or reject the read at DB2, sacrificing availability.
source: L9 slides 7-10 (CAP and replication); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.1 (CAP meaning).

question: A web application reads shopping carts almost exclusively by cart ID and wants flexible values at large scale. Which data model is the most natural primary fit?
options: A document store optimized for filtering nested cart properties across many customers, rather than direct cart-ID lookup
A graph store optimized for multi-hop relationships between shopping carts, products and customers
A key-value store optimized for fetching and updating one flexible cart value by a known cart ID
A columnar warehouse optimized for aggregate scans of purchase trends rather than individual cart writes
explanation: The key-value model directly supports access by known key and a flexible value. It does not by itself provide rich joins or arbitrary relationship traversals.
source: L9 slides 11-13 and 19 (NoSQL families and key-value stores); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.2.

question: An investigation repeatedly traverses relationships among suspects, companies, addresses and transactions. Which database model best matches the central query pattern?
options: A document store that keeps each transaction with embedded parties, requiring manual joins to traverse other documents
A graph store with explicit entity relationships and indexes for efficient multi-hop path exploration queries
A wide-column store that retrieves each suspect by row key but does not directly model linked entities
A key-value store holding each relationship list as a blob, requiring custom application traversals
explanation: Graph stores represent entities and links directly, making multi-hop traversals and pattern queries a natural operation. Simple key-value lookup has no inherent graph traversal language.
source: L9 slides 16 and 19 (graph DBMS and workload mapping); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.5.

question: Why might an enterprise prefer a NewSQL/distributed SQL system over a simple key-value store for a transactional ledger?
options: Distributed SQL can combine relational queries and transactions with scale-out, though coordination still has costs
Distributed SQL avoids transaction coordination by applying each ledger transfer as two unrelated local updates
A key-value system typically coordinates cross-record ledger operations with less complexity than relational transactions
NewSQL is mainly an OLAP interface and therefore cannot enforce operational ledger invariants across records
explanation: NewSQL aims to combine SQL/ACID-style transactional capabilities with distributed scaling. It does not eliminate costs of consensus, coordination and multi-partition operations.
source: L9 slides 18-19 (NewSQL goals and use cases); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.6.

question: What is the defining challenge a polystore addresses?
options: Making several databases use the same serialization format so their schema and query semantics become identical
Moving heterogeneous data into one fixed storage engine so a single local optimizer can execute every operation
Coordinating queries across specialized stores while handling differences in models, capabilities and placement
Keeping each store entirely isolated and issuing independent queries without reconciling any cross-store results
explanation: Polystores integrate SQL, NoSQL and other engines while retaining specialized stores. Query translation, placement of computation and heterogeneous semantics are central difficulties.
source: L9 slides 20-24 (polystores, loose/tight coupling); Özsu & Valduriez, ch. 11 §11.7.

question: Which feature is characteristic of the original Google File System (GFS) design described in the assigned distributed storage reading?
options: The master serves both metadata and bulk file payloads, while chunk servers hold only redundant recovery metadata
Clients obtain chunk locations from a master and transfer file content directly to replicated chunk servers
Clients download the full file catalogue before reading, and each chunk is stored only on the requesting client
Chunk servers centrally choose namespaces and route all file data through the master during each read request
explanation: GFS separates metadata management (master) from chunk payload storage (chunk servers). After locating chunks via the master, clients read data from chunk servers rather than routing file bytes through the master.
source: Özsu & Valduriez, Principles of Distributed Database Systems, ch. 10, printed pp. 453-456 (GFS architecture).

question: A distributed table is hash-partitioned by customer_id, but one customer produces most traffic. Why can adding workers fail to improve this workload?
options: A sufficiently strong hash function distributes each record of a hot key to a different worker without changing semantics
Adding workers reduces network cost but makes all hot-key records process in arrival order at every worker
Balanced counts of unique partition keys imply balanced traffic even if individual keys have highly unequal activity
The busiest key may remain mapped to one worker, making it the bottleneck despite unused capacity elsewhere
explanation: All records for one join/partition key may map to the same worker. That worker dominates latency, so extra idle workers provide little benefit unless the design addresses hot keys or skew.
source: L9 slides 2-4 (partitionable scale-out) and Özsu & Valduriez ch. 11 (distributed partitioning); applied reasoning.
